newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel hails U.S. pressure on PLO over Hebron deal.
newsitem.headline: Israel hails U.S. pressure on PLO over Hebron deal.

text.p: Israel on Friday welcomed U.S. pressure on the PLO to reach a deal on Israeli troop redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron, but Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said he saw no hope for an agreement.

Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh hailed remarks by U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher that put the onus on Arafat to finalise an accord. U.S. envoy Dennis Ross, mediating the Hebron talks, was due back in the region this weekend.
Arafat, upon his return to Gaza from Cairo on Friday, said he hoped Ross would be an impartial mediator and not a proponent of Israel's position.

In Hebron, a petrol bomb exploded outside a Jewish settler house, setting a laundry line on fire but causing no casualties. Arab witnesses said angry settlers rushed into the street and attacked three television cameramen, damaging their equipment.

"The Americans know full well it isn't Israel that is delaying the talks and it is now the Palestinians' turn," Naveh told Israel Radio. "I hope (Christopher's statement) and Ross's visit will help wrap up the negotiations."

In Washington on Thursday, Christopher said: "The Israelis have made some moves in connection with Hebron. We think it's time for the Palestinians, for chairman Arafat to respond to those moves, to reciprocate those moves." He gave no details.
Arafat told reporters while in Cairo he saw nothing to suggest an agreement was likely soon.
"There's no sign of hope that in the future a solution will be reached that satisfies the Palestinian side, especially in view of the Israeli government's intransigence," he said.
Asked upon his return to Gaza about a Ross visit, Arafat told reporters in English: "The most important thing is that Mr Ross has to be an accurate mediator and not to be by the side of Israel."
Arafat will travel to Jordan on Saturday for a one-day visit to consult with King Hussein on the latest developments, Arafat spokesman Nabil Abu Rdainah said.

Israel has accused Arafat of stalling in 10 weeks of talks on Hebron in hopes of bringing world pressure on right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Arafat has insisted Israel honour the agreement already signed under which about 80 percent of the town would come under Palestinian administration.
Both Christopher and U.S. President Bill Clinton voiced frustration this week with the slow pace of negotiations over the Hebron pullback, originally scheduled for last March.
Israel wants better security for 400 Jewish settlers who live or study in Hebron amid more than 100,000 Palestinians. Israel seized the West Bank in the 1967 Middle East war.
The PLO, which has denied foot-dragging, wants an Israeli commitment that implementation of peace deals signed by Israel's previous Labour-led government will not stop with the Hebron pullback.

Hebron is the last of seven West Bank towns from which Israeli troops are supposed to redeploy. Israel is also committed to hand over more West Bank land to the PLO under the deals but Palestinians fear Netanyahu will renege on it.
Netanyahu's chief of communications said in an interview published on Friday that Israel might accept a Palestinian entity called a "state" under certain conditions.
David Bar-Illan told the Jerusalem Post that Netanyahu was more concerned about the powers a Palestinian entity might have than by what it might be named.
